title: Life as a banquet
hookLine: when a dish reaches you, take a modest share; if it passes, don't reach after it (Enchiridion 15)
last: THE SLACK SHOWS UP AT THIS END.

lines: THE AUNT WHO JUST PASSES IT ON.
cards: A big family dinner. The bowls go around the table, left to right. Mashed potatoes, the good rolls, the one dish everyone fights over.
You can see it coming, four people away. An uncle has already half stood up to reach for it. A cousin watches it with her fork raised.
And one person, usually an older aunt, just talks to whoever's beside her, takes a spoonful when the bowl arrives, and passes it on. Epictetus would have liked that aunt.
Section fifteen of the handbook is set at exactly this kind of table.

teach.h: A DISH REACHES YOU: A MODEST SHARE.
teach.b: Remember, Epictetus says, to behave in life as at a banquet. A dish is carried around and reaches you: put out your hand and take a modest share.

teach.h: PASSED: DON'T HOLD IT. NOT YET: WAIT.
teach.b: It passes you by: don't hold it back. It hasn't come yet: don't send your desire out ahead to meet it. Wait until it's in front of you.
That last one is subtle. A lot of grabbing happens before anything arrives, in the head: at the promotion not yet offered, the house not yet seen, the relationship already being planned.

teach.h: CHILDREN, OFFICE, WEALTH, ON THE DISHES.
teach.b: Do the same, he says, with children, with a spouse, with office, with wealth. They come around. They pass.
Take your share well when they reach you, and you'll be a worthy guest at the banquet of the gods.

He adds a further step, for a few: if you can let some dishes go by even when they're offered, you'll share not just the gods' table but their rule. He names Diogenes the Cynic and Heraclitus as people who lived that way.
Banquet here is symposion, a drinking together, the same word as Plato's dialogue.
Ancient dinners had customs about how the dishes and the cup moved, and Epictetus turns manners everyone knew into a whole philosophy of having.
Good things come around. Take a fair share. Pass it on.
Don't lean down the table after the next bowl.

how: Some Stoic practitioners treat good things as dishes passed at a banquet: they take a moderate share when one arrives, and try not to grasp ahead or hold on as it passes.

o: a banquet: Greek for drinking together
a choir singing hymns at a temple feast
a formal debate held in a public square

games.q: life as a banquet — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says refuse every dish at the banquet
he says take a modest share; only a few, like Diogenes, let dishes go by.
he applies the banquet to children, spouse, office and wealth
they come around, and they pass.
he names Diogenes and Heraclitus as people who let offered dishes pass
and says they share the rule of the gods.

games.q: the best dish is still four seats away, and you're hungry. what does Epictetus say to do?
o: reach down the table for it.
wait until it's in front of you.
ask everyone to skip their turn.
games.why: don't send your desire ahead, he says. wait until it reaches you, then take a modest share.

practice: Think of one thing you're reaching ahead for, something that hasn't come to your end of the table yet: a trip, a result, a bit of good news.

Notice your hand, as it were, already stretched toward it, and gently bring it back to your lap. Then look at what's in front of you right now, this breath, this chair, this moment, and take a modest share of it.

wordCard.voice: Symposion, the Greek word for banquet: take a modest share when the dish reaches you, let it pass, and don't reach ahead. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 15: a banquet, literally a drinking together.

carryVoice: Your line: when the dish comes. What's in front of you is your share for now. That's day three hundred forty-seven.
